human-factors.html.Anthropometrics: Measurement of human body dimensions (from Greek: anthro = people, metrics = measure)
human-factors.html.Ergonomics: Designing for human comfort, safety, and efficiency
human-factors.html.Percentile: Statistical value showing how a measurement compares to a population
human-factors.html.Biomechanics: Study of movement and forces on the human body
human-factors.html.Physiological factors: Physical characteristics affecting performance (e.g. strength, stamina)
human-factors.html.Psychological factors: Mental processes affecting interaction (e.g. perception, memory)
human-factors.html.Static data: Measurements when the body is still
human-factors.html.Dynamic data: Measurements when the body is moving
human-factors.html.Inclusive design: Designing products accessible to as many people as possible
human-factors.html.Usability: How easy and satisfying a product is to use

psychological-factors.html.Input: Light, sound, pressure, heat, taste, or smell that enters the body
psychological-factors.html.Brain: Processes information and decides what to do
psychological-factors.html.Output: A response or action (e.g., moving your hand away from something hot)
psychological-factors.html.Visibility: Can users see it clearly? (font size, color contrast, glare)
psychological-factors.html.Readability: Is the information easy to read?
psychological-factors.html.Screen resolution: How sharp or blurry a display is
psychological-factors.html.Pitch, frequency, volume: Sound properties that affect hearing alerts/instructions
psychological-factors.html.Amplitude: Height of a sound wave; higher amplitude = louder sound
psychological-factors.html.Texture: How something feels to the touch
psychological-factors.html.Temperature: How hot or cold something feels
psychological-factors.html.Survival mechanism (taste): Bitter = warning; taste buds detect salty, bitter, sweet, umami, sour
psychological-factors.html.Emotional triggers (smell): Smells can spark memories and feelings; bad smells = warning

physiological-factors.html.Comfort: Feeling physically or psychologically at ease
physiological-factors.html.Biomechanics: How our bodies move (joints, muscles, posture, force)
physiological-factors.html.Muscle Strength: How much force we can use (changes with age!)
physiological-factors.html.Mechanical Advantage: Using tools or machines to make tasks easier
physiological-factors.html.Torque: A force that causes rotation (think: opening a jar)
physiological-factors.html.Ergonomics: Designing for human comfort, safety, and efficiency
physiological-factors.html.Inclusive Design: Designing products accessible to as many people as possible

resources-and-reserves.html.Resource: Any natural material that can be used by humans (e.g., water, wood, oil, minerals)
resources-and-reserves.html.Reserve: The known amount of a resource that can be economically and legally extracted with current technology
resources-and-reserves.html.Renewable Resource: Can be replaced naturally in a short time (e.g., solar, wind, timber)
resources-and-reserves.html.Non-renewable Resource: Cannot be replaced quickly (e.g., coal, oil, metals)
resources-and-reserves.html.Natural resources: Found in nature (e.g., water, minerals, forests)
resources-and-reserves.html.Energy resources: Sources of power (e.g., fossil fuels, wind, solar)

waste-mitigation-strategies.html.Dematerialization: Using less material and energy in products and processes
waste-mitigation-strategies.html.Embodied energy: Total energy used to make, transport, use, and dispose of a product
waste-mitigation-strategies.html.Reuse: Using a product again for the same or a new purpose
waste-mitigation-strategies.html.Repair: Fixing a product to extend its life
waste-mitigation-strategies.html.Recondition: Restoring a product to like-new condition
waste-mitigation-strategies.html.Re-engineer: Redesigning to improve efficiency or reduce material/energy use

waste-mitigation-methods.html.Product recovery: Getting useful materials or energy back from waste
waste-mitigation-methods.html.Reuse: Using products again for the same or new purpose
waste-mitigation-methods.html.Reduce: Using fewer resources and less energy
waste-mitigation-methods.html.Material substitution: Replacing materials with more sustainable options
waste-mitigation-methods.html.Energy efficiency: Using less energy to do the same work
waste-mitigation-methods.html.Quality assurance: Ensuring products meet standards during production
waste-mitigation-methods.html.Circular economy: Keeping resources in use for as long as possible

batteries.html.Battery: Device that stores chemical energy and converts it to electrical energy
batteries.html.Anode: The negative electrode where oxidation occurs
batteries.html.Cathode: The positive electrode where reduction occurs
batteries.html.Electrolyte: Substance that allows ions to move between electrodes
batteries.html.Capacitor: Device that stores and releases electrical energy quickly
batteries.html.Alkaline: Common in AA/AAA, sometimes rechargeable, more recyclable
batteries.html.Lithium Ion: Rechargeable, used in phones, laptops, electric cars
batteries.html.Lead Acid: Rechargeable, used in car engines, delivers high voltage
batteries.html.Nickel Iron: Invented by Edison, durable, less common
batteries.html.Nickel Metal Hydride: Rechargeable, used in hybrid cars and electronics

energy-utilization.html.Energy utilization: How energy is used, stored, and distributed
energy-utilization.html.Embodied energy: Total energy used to make, transport, use, and dispose of a product
energy-utilization.html.Carbon footprint: Total greenhouse gases produced by a product or activity
energy-utilization.html.Renewable energy: Energy from sources that are naturally replenished (solar, wind, hydro)
energy-utilization.html.Non-renewable energy: Energy from sources that can run out (coal, oil, gas, nuclear)
energy-utilization.html.Cradle to grave: The full life cycle of a product, from creation to disposal
energy-utilization.html.Megajoule (MJ): A unit of energy (1 million joules)
energy-utilization.html.kg CO₂/kg: Kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of material

energy-distribution.html.Power grid: Network for delivering electricity from producers to consumers
energy-distribution.html.Local generation: Producing energy close to where it's used
energy-distribution.html.CHP (Combined Heat & Power): Plants that generate both heat and electricity for local use
energy-distribution.html.Embodied carbon: Total greenhouse gases released during a product's life cycle
energy-distribution.html.Greenhouse gas: Gases that trap heat in the atmosphere (CO₂, methane, etc.)
energy-distribution.html.Global warming potential (GWP): How much a gas contributes to global warming compared to CO₂

clean-technology.html.Clean technology: Products, services, or processes that reduce waste and use fewer non-renewable resources
clean-technology.html.Service: Non-physical product (like banking, streaming, food delivery)
clean-technology.html.Process: How something is made or done (manufacturing, energy generation)
clean-technology.html.Legislation: Laws that require or encourage clean tech
clean-technology.html.Community pressure: When people or groups push for cleaner practices
clean-technology.html.International treaty: Agreements between countries to protect the environment
clean-technology.html.Vision 2030: Saudi Arabia's plan to diversify its economy and reduce oil dependence

concept-modeling.html.Conceptual model: An idea or mental model to help understand and solve problems
concept-modeling.html.Ideation: Generating lots of ideas for solutions
concept-modeling.html.Iteration: Repeating and improving ideas over time
concept-modeling.html.Prototype: A physical or virtual model built to test ideas
concept-modeling.html.Communication: Sharing ideas with others (team, client, manufacturer)

physical-modeling.html.Physical model: A 3D model made to test, explore, or communicate a design
physical-modeling.html.Scale model: A model that is proportionally smaller or larger than the real object
physical-modeling.html.Mock-up: A scale or full-size model used to gain feedback, may have some functionality
physical-modeling.html.Aesthetic model: Looks like the real product but doesn't function
physical-modeling.html.Prototype: A working model that functions like the final product
physical-modeling.html.Instrumented model: A prototype with sensors to collect data
physical-modeling.html.Fidelity: How closely a model matches the final product (low, medium, high)

computer-aided-design.html.CAD: Computer-Aided Design: using software to create, modify, analyze, or optimize a design
computer-aided-design.html.2D modeling: Flat drawings (length & width), e.g., Adobe Illustrator, AutoCAD
computer-aided-design.html.3D modeling: Digital objects with length, width, and depth, e.g., Fusion 360, SketchUp, SolidWorks
computer-aided-design.html.Rendering: Making a 3D model look real with lighting, textures, and shadows (e.g., Blender, 3DS Max)
computer-aided-design.html.Surface model: Realistic image of a product's exterior, no interior data
computer-aided-design.html.Solid model: Includes both exterior and interior data (volume, structure)
computer-aided-design.html.Data model: Organizes and structures data, often for IT systems
computer-aided-design.html.Virtual prototyping: Interactive digital mock-ups for testing and feedback

rapid-prototyping.html.Rapid prototyping: Quickly producing a complete product (with internal detail) using digital tools
rapid-prototyping.html.Additive manufacturing: Building up a product by adding material (e.g., 3D printing)
rapid-prototyping.html.Subtractive manufacturing: Creating a product by removing material (e.g., milling)
rapid-prototyping.html.3D printing: Additive process that builds objects layer by layer
rapid-prototyping.html.Milling: Subtractive process that removes material using a rotating tool
rapid-prototyping.html.CNC: Computer Numerical Control; machines controlled by computers (e.g., CNC router)
rapid-prototyping.html.Axis (axes): Directions of movement (X, Y, Z); 3-axis or 5-axis machines
rapid-prototyping.html.Resin: Liquid material hardened by light in some 3D printers

advanced-cad-tech.html.Bottom-up design: Creating all parts separately, then assembling (e.g., piston)
advanced-cad-tech.html.Top-down design: Designing the overall shape first, then fitting components inside (e.g., car body)
advanced-cad-tech.html.Digital humans: Computer models simulating human mechanics/biology for testing (e.g., pilot reach)
advanced-cad-tech.html.Motion capture: Recording real human movement for animation (e.g., Andy Serkis as Gollum)
advanced-cad-tech.html.Haptic technology: Tech that simulates touch/force feedback (e.g., VR suits, game controllers)
advanced-cad-tech.html.Virtual reality (VR): Simulating real situations on screen, interactively
advanced-cad-tech.html.Animation: Linking graphics to simulate motion or process
advanced-cad-tech.html.Finite element analysis (FEA): Simulating stresses/forces in products using CAD

additive-manufacturing-tech.html.Stereolithography (SLA): Additive process using UV laser to harden resin layer by layer
additive-manufacturing-tech.html.Laminated Object Manufacturing (LOM): Laser cuts and stacks sheets of material to build up an object
additive-manufacturing-tech.html.Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM): 3D printing technique that melts and deposits layers of material (e.g., plastic, concrete)
additive-manufacturing-tech.html.Selective Laser Sintering (SLS): Laser fuses powder particles into a solid 3D shape
additive-manufacturing-tech.html.Filament: Material (often plastic) melted in FDM 3D printing
additive-manufacturing-tech.html.Resin: Liquid material hardened by light in SLA 3D printing
additive-manufacturing-tech.html.Powder: Fine material fused by laser in SLS
additive-manufacturing-tech.html.Layers: Thin slices added one at a time to build up a 3D object

properties-of-materials.html.Density: Mass per unit volume (g/cm³ or kg/m³)
properties-of-materials.html.Electrical resistivity: How well a material resists electrical flow
properties-of-materials.html.Thermal conductivity: How well a material conducts heat
properties-of-materials.html.Thermal expansion: How much a material expands when heated
properties-of-materials.html.Ductility: Ability to be drawn into wire or extended shape
properties-of-materials.html.Aesthetics: How a material looks, feels, smells, or tastes

invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Invention: Discovering a new principle that leads to a novel product
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Motivators for invention: Personal interest, constructive discontent, money, scientific curiosity, necessity
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Lone inventor: Someone working (often alone) on a novel product, sometimes isolated
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Intellectual property (IP): Legal rights for creations of the mind (inventions, designs, etc.)
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Patent: Government-granted right to make/sell an invention for a set time
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Copyright: Legal right for creators to control use/distribution of their work
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Trademark: Symbol, word, or phrase legally registered to represent a company/product
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Public domain: When copyright expires or is given up; anyone can use the work
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.First to market: First product of its type released; can make the most money
invention-and-intellectual-property.html.Shelf technology: Tech that's developed but not released until later
